trial_name: SONIA — Adjunctive Glucocorticoids for Community-Acquired Pneumonia (2025)
citation: Lucinde RK, Gathuri H, Mwaniki P, et al. A Pragmatic Trial of Glucocorticoids for Community-Acquired Pneumonia. N Engl J Med. 2025;393(22):2187-2197
one_liner: In adults with clinical CAP in Kenyan public hospitals, adjunctive low-dose glucocorticoids reduced 30-day mortality (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.73–0.97).

pico.population: Adults ≥18 years admitted within 48 hours with clinician-diagnosed CAP in Kenyan public hospitals
pico.intervention: Standard care plus adjunctive low-dose systemic glucocorticoids (prednisolone-equivalent 50 mg once daily) for up to 10 days

background.existing_knowledge: CAP is a major cause of morbidity and mortality, with disproportionately high case-fatality in sub-Saharan Africa despite a younger patient population. Glucocorticoids are biologically plausible adjuncts in CAP, targeting harmful host inflammatory responses that contribute to respiratory failure and shock. Prior RCTs and meta-analyses (largely high-income, often ICU-enriched) suggested possible reductions in mortality and clinical deterioration, but effect estimates varied by severity, steroid class/dose, and concomitant care. In many African settings, ward-based care predominates and ICU access is constrained, creating uncertainty about the applicability of ICU-centric steroid evidence to routine inpatient care.
background.knowledge_gap: Applicability of ICU-centric steroid evidence to routine inpatient CAP care in LMIC settings.
background.hypothesis: Adjunctive glucocorticoids would reduce time-to-death risk over 30 days compared with standard care.

methods.design: Pragmatic, open-label, individually randomised, multicentre, parallel-group trial across 18 public hospitals in Kenya.
methods.setting: General wards (HDU/ICU eligible but uncommon); enrolled Jun 2018–Aug 2022.

inclusion: Clinician diagnosis of CAP (≥2 symptoms/signs for <14 days: cough, fever, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, chest pain, or crackles)
Written consent or deferred consent where too unwell
exclusion: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (>48h without symptoms at admission)
Known/suspected condition requiring glucocorticoids (COPD, asthma, adrenal insufficiency, PCP)
Confirmed COVID-19 or strong clinical suspicion prompting steroid use

methods.intervention: Standard care plus adjunctive low-dose systemic glucocorticoids for up to 10 days (prednisolone-equivalent 50 mg once daily). Formulations: betamethasone 5 mg, dexamethasone 6 mg, hydrocortisone 160 mg, methylprednisolone 30 mg, prednisolone 50 mg, prednisone 50 mg (choice by randomisation and availability). Route: oral (including NG) preferred; IV if oral unavailable. Median time to first dose: 1 day; median in-hospital duration: 4 days.
methods.comparison: Standard care: clinician-directed antibiotics (e.g., beta-lactam + macrolide) and supportive care. Open-label glucocorticoids permitted if later clinically indicated (recorded as withdrawals).
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 2180 participants to detect 5% absolute reduction in 30-day mortality (20% to 15%) with 85% power at two-sided α=0.05, allowing ~5% loss; primary analysis intention-to-treat.
methods.follow_up: 30 days post-randomisation (phone follow-up at day 14 and day 30).

headline_bullets: Adjunctive glucocorticoids reduced 30-day all-cause mortality compared with standard care (22.6% vs 26.0%; HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.73–0.97; P=0.02).
Mortality reduction appeared early (by day 7) and persisted through day 30; sensitivity analyses were consistent.
ICU transfer rates were very low (<0.3% in both arms), reflecting a ward-based, resource-limited context.
Adverse events were broadly similar; hyperglycaemia events were more frequent with glucocorticoids (35 vs 3 events).

outcomes_table.note: Reflects very low ICU access/transfer in this setting
62/211 events (29.4%) in glucocorticoid arm judged related
5 patients (0.5%) had events judged related to glucocorticoids
Reported as adverse-event counts, not unique patients

safety: Hyperglycaemia events: 35 vs 3 (event counts, not unique patients)
Adverse events judged related to glucocorticoids: 29.4% of events in intervention arm
Serious adverse events judged related to glucocorticoids: 5 patients (0.5%)

domains.notes: Site-specific computer-generated block randomisation; allocation concealment via tablet-based system with opaque envelopes as backup.
Open-label design may introduce performance bias and differential withdrawal; primary outcome (mortality) is objective, partially mitigating detection bias.
8.9% withdrawn by day 30 (8.1% vs 9.7%); missingness not MCAR (Little’s test P<0.001) but non-differential by arm; sensitivity analyses concordant.
97.6% of intervention arm received glucocorticoids; 3.0% of control arm received non-trial glucocorticoids; moderate contamination but high adherence overall.
Groups well balanced on demographics, severity, and comorbidities.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate internal validity: open-label design and withdrawals introduce bias, but objective outcome and concordant sensitivity analyses support the primary mortality finding.

domains.notes: Adults with clinically defined CAP in Kenyan public hospitals, including prevalent HIV, resembling real-world LMIC general ward settings.
High for LMIC ward-based CAP with limited ICU access; limited applicability to high-resource ICU severe CAP.

external_validity.verdict: High for LMIC ward-based CAP care similar to the Kenyan trial sites; limited for high-resource ICU contexts.

strengths: Large, pragmatic, multicentre trial in a high-mortality, understudied setting
Objective, patient-centred primary outcome (30-day all-cause mortality) with time-to-event analysis
High delivery of allocated intervention (97.6%) and high antibiotic use in both arms
Prespecified sensitivity analyses and model checks (including proportional hazards testing)
limitations: Open-label design with potential performance bias and withdrawal-related bias (including non-trial steroid initiation)
Clinical (not microbiologic) CAP definition and limited radiography increase diagnostic heterogeneity
Heterogeneous glucocorticoid formulations and mid-trial formulation changes complicate attribution to a single agent
Planned 10-day exposure frequently truncated in-hospital (median 4 days); post-discharge adherence unverified

critical_appraisal.summary: SONIA provides moderate-quality evidence that adjunctive glucocorticoids reduce 30-day mortality in clinically diagnosed CAP in a LMIC ward setting, but open-label design and exposure heterogeneity limit certainty.

sections.authors_conclusion: In Kenyan inpatients with clinical CAP, adjunctive low-dose glucocorticoids were associated with lower 30-day mortality than standard care alone (HR 0.84; 95% CI 0.73 to 0.97).

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This landmark trial supports use of adjunctive low-dose glucocorticoids in hospitalised adults with CAP in LMIC settings where ICU access is limited.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adults admitted with clinical CAP to general wards in resource-limited settings, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: The findings do not necessarily apply to severe ICU-managed CAP in high-income countries, or to patients with alternative steroid-responsive conditions (e.g., TB, PCP).
implementation_caveats: Requires capacity for glucose monitoring due to increased hyperglycaemia risk
Must differentiate CAP from steroid-sensitive or contraindicated diagnoses (e.g., TB, heart failure)
Oral, once-daily dosing is scalable but short in-hospital exposure may limit effect

controversies.notes: Clinical CAP definition without routine microbiologic/radiographic confirmation may include syndromes where steroids could help, harm, or be neutral, complicating generalization.
Protocol used multiple equivalent-dose glucocorticoids; hydrocortisone and prednisone were removed during trial due to pill burden, reducing precision for formulation-level inference.

controversies.topic: Contrast with ICU severe CAP trials
controversies.notes: CAPE COD found mortality reduction with hydrocortisone in severe ICU CAP, supporting benefit in high-resource severe-CAP; SONIA extends the signal to ward-based LMIC. REMAP-CAP found futility for hydrocortisone in severe CAP corticosteroid domain, highlighting persistent uncertainty about which CAP phenotypes benefit.

A 2024 non-viral CAP meta-analysis supports overall mortality reduction with corticosteroids but emphasises heterogeneity; SONIA will materially influence future pooled estimates because of its size and LMIC setting.

2024 SCCM focused update recommends corticosteroids for severe CAP, while others restrict to critical care; SONIA’s LMIC ward data may shift recommendations. Formal updates incorporating SONIA not yet identified.
Hyperglycaemia more frequent with glucocorticoids (35 vs 3 events); serious adverse events similar overall; implementation should include pragmatic glucose monitoring.

context_related_trials.relation: ICU severe CAP trial showing mortality benefit with hydrocortisone; SONIA extends the signal to ward-based LMIC CAP.
Found futility for hydrocortisone in severe CAP, suggesting uncertain benefit and highlighting context dependence; SONIA’s positive result in a different setting adds complexity.
Pooled analysis supporting overall mortality reduction; SONIA will likely strengthen this signal.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal steroid agent and duration in CAP?
Can diagnostic algorithms reliably exclude TB/PCP in settings with limited resources to avoid harm?
Is the benefit consistent in severe CAP with high-resource ICU care?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In ward-based CAP in resource-limited settings, a short course of low-dose glucocorticoids reduced 30-day mortality with a number needed to treat of about 30.
